value.overview: The Brown-billed Scythebill is a specialized woodcreeper of humid forests in Central and South America. Its most distinctive feature is an unusually long, strongly down-curved bill, used while climbing trunks and vines in search of small prey. It is generally unobtrusive and often detected by its voice or by watching mixed-species feeding flocks. In Costa Rica, it is an uncommon resident of forested mountain regions and nearby humid lowlands.
value.classification: The Brown-billed Scythebill belongs to the ovenbird family Furnariidae and the woodcreeper subfamily Dendrocolaptinae. Its scientific name is Campylorhamphus pusillus.
value.identification: This medium-sized woodcreeper is mainly warm brown above, with fine pale streaking on the head, throat, and upper breast. The underparts become less heavily marked toward the belly. The wings and tail are generally rufous, while the bill is long, slender, brownish, and extremely decurved. It climbs trunks and large vines in a woodpecker-like manner. Its stuttering or broken whistled series can help distinguish it from other woodcreepers.
value.rangeHabitat: The species occurs from Costa Rica and Panama south through the Andes of Colombia, Venezuela, Ecuador, and Peru. In Costa Rica, it is a localized, uncommon resident on the Caribbean-facing slopes of the Cordillera de Tilarán, the Central Volcanic Cordillera, and the Talamanca range, generally from about 300 to 1,500 meters. It also occurs on the southwestern Pacific slope, especially in the General-Térraba-Coto Brus region and humid foothills near the Golfo Dulce. It favors dense, humid evergreen and cloud forest, including forest edges and some mature secondary growth.
value.migrationStatus: The Brown-billed Scythebill is considered a year-round resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range. Regular long-distance migration is not known, although limited local or elevational movements may occur, particularly in Central America.
value.breeding: The species is believed to form monogamous pairs during breeding. In Costa Rica, recently fledged young have been observed mainly from May through July, suggesting breeding in the early wet season, although the full breeding calendar is not well documented. Nest details are poorly known compared with those of many other woodcreepers. Adults apparently place nests in natural cavities or other sheltered spaces associated with trunks, branches, or dense forest vegetation.
value.dietFeeding: The Brown-billed Scythebill feeds mainly on arthropods, including insects and other small invertebrates found beneath bark, among mosses, and in tangled vines. It usually forages alone or in pairs, moving upward along trunks and limbs while probing crevices with its curved bill. It also frequently joins mixed-species feeding flocks, especially in the understory and lower levels of the forest canopy.
value.behavior: This species is generally solitary and inconspicuous. It grips rough bark with strong feet and uses its stiff tail as support while hitching upward along trunks and vines. Individuals may pause to give a series of sharp or stuttering notes. In Costa Rica, it is often encountered in mature humid forest, forest edges, and mixed-species flocks. Its slow, trunk-climbing foraging style contrasts with the more active movements of many canopy birds.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not clearly quantified, but the species is not currently considered globally threatened.
